extracted.intended_audience: aspiring and practicing writers of suspense fiction (novels and short stories)
extracted.subtask_description: Guidance for plotting, characterization, tone, and craft specific to suspense fiction (including criminal-protagonist work), with practical advice on idea development, description, and revision.

rubrics_metrics.name: Art has nothing to do with morality, convention, or moralizing
rubrics_metrics.description: "Art has nothing to do with morality, convention, or moralizing."
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Highsmith's stance: do not let moralizing dictate artistic choices; she embraced criminal protagonists (e.g., Tom Ripley) and allows morally ambiguous or monstrous characters to be central without authorial moral judgment.

rubrics_metrics.name: Suspense doesn't need tricks
rubrics_metrics.description: "Well-written" suspense doesn't need formula. Strong plotting + well-rounded characters carry it.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Avoid gimmicks or formulaic devices; rely on solid plotting and fully realized characters to generate suspense organically.

rubrics_metrics.name: Likeable criminal protagonists
rubrics_metrics.description: When making a psychopath/criminal protagonist likeable, give them as many pleasant qualities as possible — generosity, kindness to certain people, fondness for the arts, refined taste.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Make the protagonist enjoyable to spend time with even when monstrous; use pleasant, humanizing traits to create reader engagement and complicity.

rubrics_metrics.name: Let ideas incubate (idea development)
rubrics_metrics.description: Once you have an idea, let it sit — let the subconscious develop it. Then add character, setting, atmosphere.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Allow ideas time to mature before forcing plot; use incubation to discover richer character and setting details that inform plot choices.

rubrics_metrics.name: Description by implication (use telling details)
rubrics_metrics.description: "Don't describe everything in a room, but use a few words to depict a room as rich, poor, neat, careless, fussy, masculine or feminine."
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Prefer a few telling details over exhaustive inventory; choose details that imply social class, personality, mood, or history.

rubrics_metrics.name: Plot from character under pressure
rubrics_metrics.description: Plot emerges from putting interesting characters in pressure situations and watching them choose.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Drive story events by authentic character decisions under stress rather than by contrived external plot mechanics.

rubrics_metrics.name: Tone: conversational, not prescriptive
rubrics_metrics.description: Highsmith's tone is conversational, not prescriptive. "Here's how I did it" not "here's the rule."
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Adopt a voice that shares craft as personal method and example rather than issuing hard rules; show rather than preach.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use coincidence sparingly
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Avoid overreliance on coincidence to resolve plot problems; when coincidence appears, it should feel plausible and not undermine causal setup.

rubrics_metrics.name: Characterization with moral ambiguity
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Develop characters whose motives and ethics are complex; moral ambiguity can deepen suspense and reader engagement, particularly with criminal protagonists.

rubrics_metrics.name: Drafting and revision
rubrics_metrics.description: Drafting and revision are essential parts of the process.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Iterate on drafts—develop ideas, then refine character, plot, and language through revision rather than expecting a finished form on first pass.

rubrics_metrics.name: Reader anticipation drives suspense
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Design scenes and sequences to create and maintain anticipation; suspense is generated by what the reader expects to happen and the delay/uncertainty about that outcome.

rubrics_metrics.name: Withhold information strategically
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Control the flow of facts to the reader to sustain tension—reveal deliberately to heighten stakes and complicity.

rubrics_metrics.name: Ratchet up consequences (escalation)
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Increase the stakes progressively so that each decision or reveal has greater impact; escalation maintains momentum and suspense.

rubrics_metrics.name: Make the reader complicit
rubrics_metrics.description: Make the reader complicit (especially in criminal-protagonist work).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Invite readers into the protagonist's perspective or secret knowledge so they feel morally implicated; this deepens tension and emotional investment.

rubrics_metrics.name: Surprises must be earned by setup
rubrics_metrics.description: Surprises must be earned by setup.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Ensure twists and surprises follow from earlier clues or developments; avoid shocks that lack prior justification or foreshadowing.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid deus ex machina rescues
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Do not resolve problems with implausible or external rescues; endings should arise from established characters, choices, and plot logic.

rubrics_metrics.name: Endings should disturb rather than reassure
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Prefer unsettling or ambiguous closings that leave a psychological or moral residue over tidy, reassuring resolutions—especially in suspense traditions that foreground moral ambiguity.
